extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; literate general public and essayists interested in moral/satirical discourse
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing moral and satirical essays: how to direct satire responsibly, how to judge actions by intentions, persuasive strategies for moral writing, and social rules for patron-client relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire should expose only corrigible faults and discriminate targets
rubrics_metrics.description: A Satyr should expose nothing but what is corrigible, and make a due Discrimination between those who are, and those who are not the proper Objects of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'levelling Satyrs' that condemn an entire sex or species (these are 'of no Use to the World'). The author praises Simonides for distinguishing among individuals rather than attacking the whole sex, and criticizes Juvenal and Boileau for indiscriminate invective. Satire's purpose is correction, so it must single out what can be amended and not mock the ineradicable or indiscriminately malign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral evaluation by classification of actions and intentions
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide actions into those that are Good, Evil, or Indifferent; likewise consider intentions as Good, Evil, or Indifferent; the moral value of an action depends on the combination of intention and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit combinations given: a good intention joined to a good action gives it proper force and efficacy; a good intention joined to an evil action may extenuate its malignity or in some cases take it away; a good intention joined to an indifferent action turns it to a virtue. An evil intention perverts the best actions and makes indifferent actions sinful; an indifferent intention destroys the merit of a good action and lessens but does not remove the malignity of an evil action. Use this matrix when judging conduct or composing moral argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate habitual good intention to render actions meritorious
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of unspeakable advantage to possess our Minds with an habitual good Intention, and to aim all our Thoughts, Words, and Actions at some laudable End.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this habit as 'thrift or good‑husbandry' in moral life: by applying a good intention even to indifferent actions you multiply opportunities for virtue ('make our very Existence one continued Act of Obedience'). This is a prescriptive standard for authors and moral agents: encourage readers to adopt a constant, virtuous aim so that ordinary actions contribute to moral life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasive strategy: recommend virtue via pagan/ancient examples
rubrics_metrics.description: When treating moral subjects, recommend the virtue by the Precepts or Examples of the ancient Heathens to shame those who have greater advantages of knowing their Duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rhetorical tactic is used because many readers are more inclined to give a fair hearing to a Pagan Philosopher than to a Christian Writer. Invoking admired ancient figures (Socrates, classical examples) can embarrass better‑informed or privileged readers into improving conduct; use classical exempla to increase receptivity and moral pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patron-client ethical standard: obligations and unjust patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: He who will take up another's Time and Fortune in his Service, though he has no Prospect of rewarding his Merit towards him, is as unjust in his Dealings as he who takes up Goods of a Tradesman without Intention or Ability to pay him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat patronage as a debt of honour that ought to be discharged first; patrons should not promise or accept homage if they lack the ability or intention to reward. The essay warns of the long-term ruin of dependants who wait fruitlessly and counsels caution about entering leagues where power and obligation are absent. Use this as an ethical standard for evaluating social arrangements and narrating examples of injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical strategies for gaining favour of the great: be considerable or agreeable
rubrics_metrics.description: There are but two Ways of doing any thing with great People, and those are by making your self either considerable or agreeable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be 'considerable' requires independence (living without them) or concealing your need for them; to be 'agreeable' requires conforming to their tastes—even imitating faults or complying with vices—an often servile course. This is pragmatic advice for dependants seeking advancement: choose the route of self-sufficiency or conscious adaptiveness, and be aware of the moral cost of ingratiation.
